Q65.t: A city poured into a basin between peaks and the Pacific
Q65.s: Los Angeles doesn't so much end as run out of room: its sprawl fills a broad basin from the Pacific shore to the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains, then spills into the valleys beyond. In winter those peaks can wear snow above a city of palm trees. It all began in 1781 as a small Spanish farming pueblo.
Q65.w: A vast grey-beige sprawl between mountains and Santa Monica Bay; the long harbour breakwaters of Long Beach to the south.
f: The Los Angeles River runs mostly in a concrete channel, lined from the 1930s onward to tame its floods.
The neighbouring ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach together form the busiest container port complex in the US.
The highest of the San Gabriels, Mount San Antonio (about 3,070 m), is known locally as Mount Baldy.

q.q: Which mountain range walls in Los Angeles to the north?

Q61.t: A capital drawn on paper first, then built on the Potomac
Q61.s: Washington was planned before it existed: in 1791 Pierre L'Enfant laid broad diagonal avenues over a street grid on farmland beside the Potomac. The district began as a square ten miles a side, set on its corner like a diamond. Virginia took back its share in 1846, so today the river bites off the south-west corner.
Q61.w: Where the Anacostia meets the broad Potomac; a low city without a skyscraper cluster, Reagan National airport right on the riverbank.
f: Forty stone markers were set along the original diamond-shaped boundary in 1791–92; many still stand.
Congress first met in Washington in 1800.
A law of 1910 caps building heights, which is why the city looks so strikingly low.

q.q: Which river forms Washington's south-western edge?

Q60.t: Look for the green rectangle in the middle of the island
Q60.s: Find Manhattan — a long, thin island between the Hudson and the East River — and in its middle a neat green rectangle: Central Park, about four kilometres long. Around it the street grid laid out in 1811 runs block after block up the island. The Dutch called this port New Amsterdam until the English took it in 1664 and renamed it after the Duke of York.
Q60.w: A narrow island pointing south into a wide harbour, a green rectangle at its heart, long bridges fanning out to the east.
f: Central Park measures about 4 km by 0.8 km — big enough to pick out from cruise on a clear day.
The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge at the harbour mouth had the world's longest suspension span when it opened in 1964.
Manhattan's street grid was fixed by a plan of 1811, long before most of the island was built up.

q.q: What was New York called before 1664?

Q1489.t: A megacity on a lake that isn't there any more
Q1489.s: The grey-brown sea of roofs below fills an old lake bed 2,240 m above sea level. The Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco around 1325; the Spanish later drained most of the water. The clay beneath is still settling, and parts of the city sink every year. On a clear day, look south-east for two snow-capped volcanoes.
Q1489.w: A vast city filling a flat high valley ringed by mountains; Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl rise to the south-east.
f: Popocatépetl, about 5,400 m high, is an active volcano and often trails a plume of steam.
In places the city sinks by more than 20 cm a year as the old lake clay dries out.
Iztaccíhuatl means 'white woman' in Nahuatl, and its long ridge is said to look like a sleeping figure.

q.q: What did Mexico City's centre stand on in Aztec times?

Q2841.t: A capital at 2,640 m, pressed against a green mountain wall
Q2841.s: Bogotá lies on a high, flat savanna in the Andes, about 2,640 m up, with a steep ridge of hills along its eastern edge. The city fills the plain westward from that wall. Look around it for glinting white patches: greenhouses of the flower farms that make Colombia one of the world's great exporters of cut flowers.
Q2841.w: A large city on a flat green plateau, hard against a dark ridge to the east; white greenhouse roofs scattered across the fields.
f: The Spanish conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada founded the city in 1538.
The legend of El Dorado grew from a Muisca ritual at Lake Guatavita, about 50 km north-east of the city.
Monserrate, the hill above the old town, rises to about 3,150 m.

q.q: At which lake did the El Dorado legend begin?

Q2887.t: A city in a bowl, with the Andes rising straight behind
Q2887.s: Santiago fills a broad valley between the low Coastal Range and the Andes, which climb to snowy peaks over 5,000 m just east of the suburbs. In winter a haze often pools in the bowl while the summits shine above it. Pedro de Valdivia founded the city in 1541 beside a rocky hill on the Mapocho River.
Q2887.w: A large city on a flat valley floor at the foot of the Andes' snowy wall; the thin line of the Mapocho River across it.
f: Aconcagua, at 6,961 m the highest peak outside Asia, stands about 100 km north-east of the city.
Cerro Santa Lucía, the hill where the city was founded, is now a park in the very centre.
The border with Argentina follows the crest of the Andes less than 100 km from the city.

q.q: Who founded Santiago in 1541?

Q8678.t: Green granite domes rising straight out of the sea
Q8678.s: Few cities are so tangled up with rock: steep, forested granite domes rise between the neighbourhoods and straight out of Guanabara Bay. Portuguese sailors arrived in January 1502 and took the bay for a river mouth — hence 'River of January'. From 1808 to 1821 the Portuguese court lived here, a European monarchy ruling its empire from the Americas.
Q8678.w: A wide bay with a narrow mouth, green domes of rock among the buildings, and long pale beaches facing the open Atlantic.
f: The Rio–Niterói Bridge crosses Guanabara Bay for about 13 km; from cruise it's a fine line over the water.
Much of the Tijuca Forest above the city was replanted by hand from the 1860s on old coffee land.
Sugarloaf Mountain rises about 396 m straight from the water at the mouth of the bay.

q.q: Which bay does the Rio–Niterói Bridge cross?

Q174.t: The Southern Hemisphere's biggest city, up on a plateau
Q174.s: From the window São Paulo looks endless: grey and white rooftops to the horizon, stitched together by rivers in straight concrete channels. It sits on a plateau about 760 m up, only some 70 km from the Atlantic, behind the steep forested wall of the Serra do Mar. Jesuit missionaries founded it as a small mission in 1554.
Q174.w: A boundless grey city; large dark reservoirs on its southern edge, the green escarpment and the coast beyond to the south-east.
f: The Tietê River rises near the coast yet flows inland, over 1,000 km, to join the Paraná.
The Billings and Guarapiranga reservoirs on the southern edge are easy to spot from cruise.
The coffee trade of the 1800s turned a modest hill town into Brazil's economic engine.

q.q: Which way does the Tietê River flow from São Paulo?
x: East, to the Atlantic at Santos

Q62.t: A hilly peninsula tip where fog pours through the Gate
Q62.s: San Francisco fills the tip of a peninsula, with the Pacific on one side and a great bay on the other, joined by the narrow Golden Gate. On summer afternoons you may see fog pouring through that gap like a slow white river. The gold rush of 1849 turned a village of about a thousand people into a boom town within a couple of years.
Q62.w: A peninsula tip between ocean and bay; thin bridge lines across the water; bright red and green salt ponds far to the south.
f: The salt ponds of the south bay glow red, orange and green, coloured by salt-loving microorganisms.
The Golden Gate strait was named in 1846, almost a century before the famous bridge was built.
Mission San Francisco de Asís, the city's Spanish seed, was founded in 1776.

q.q: What colours the salt ponds of south San Francisco Bay?

Q16554.t: Where the Great Plains run into the Rockies
Q16554.s: Denver marks the line where the flat country stops: to the east the plains roll away for a thousand kilometres, to the west the Front Range rises in a wall of peaks over 4,000 m. The city grew from a gold-rush camp of 1858 and sits about a mile above sea level — hence its nickname, the Mile High City.
Q16554.w: A city on flat tan plains at the very foot of the Rockies; its huge airport stands alone far out to the north-east.
f: Denver International is the largest airport in North America by land area, about 135 km².
The city was named after James W. Denver, governor of Kansas Territory, which then included the site.
Longs Peak, about 4,350 m high, is the prominent summit on the north-western skyline.

q.q: What brought the first settlers to Denver in 1858?

Q16555.t: Bayous, refineries and a ship channel on a flat plain
Q16555.s: Houston spreads across a coastal plain so flat that its slow brown bayous wander in loops through the suburbs. Look south-east for the Ship Channel, a dredged waterway of about 80 km lined with refineries and tanks, running out to Galveston Bay. Founded in 1836, the city was named after Sam Houston, hero of Texan independence.
Q16555.w: Endless flat sprawl ringed by freeway loops; to the south-east, a waterway lined with industry leading to a wide bay.
f: Houston is famous as the largest US city without a formal zoning code.
NASA's Mission Control for crewed spaceflight is in the city's south-eastern suburbs.
At night the refineries along the Ship Channel glitter as a long, dense band of light.

q.q: Who is Houston named after?

Q8652.t: A thin city between the Everglades and turquoise water
Q8652.s: Miami is a long, narrow city pinned between two very different edges: the pale green marshes of the Everglades to the west and the turquoise shallows of Biscayne Bay to the east. Beyond the bay runs the thin barrier island of Miami Beach. The city was incorporated only in 1896, just after Henry Flagler's railway arrived.
Q8652.w: A strip of city along the coast; a straight line where streets stop and marsh begins; a bright ribbon of island offshore.
f: Much of Miami lies only a couple of metres above sea level, on porous limestone.
Miami Beach was largely mangrove swamp before it was cleared and built up in the 1910s and 1920s.
The chain of small Venetian Islands across Biscayne Bay is largely man-made.

q.q: Which wetland lies directly west of Miami?

Q23556.t: Towers in a forest, beside a giant of an airport
Q23556.s: Atlanta looks surprisingly green from above: a thick canopy of trees hides most of its suburbs, with clusters of towers rising out of it. South of downtown, look for the long parallel runways of Hartsfield–Jackson, for many years the world's busiest airport by passengers. The city began in 1837 as the end point of a railway, simply named Terminus.
Q23556.w: Clusters of towers in dense green forest; a huge airport with parallel east–west runways to the south; a pale granite dome to the east.
f: Stone Mountain, a bare granite dome east of the city, rises about 250 m above the surrounding forest.
The Eastern Continental Divide crosses Atlanta: rain on one side flows to the Atlantic, on the other to the Gulf.
The name Atlanta was adopted in 1845, after a brief spell as Marthasville.

q.q: What was Atlanta called when it began in 1837?

Q1297.t: A perfect grid ruled against a lake like an inland sea
Q1297.s: Chicago's edge is one long, straight line: Lake Michigan, so wide that from the ground its far shore lies beyond the horizon. Inland the streets run in a strict grid, and at night it glows orange, block by block, far out across the prairie. The city exists because of a short portage here between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi basin.
Q1297.w: A huge city on the south-west shore of Lake Michigan; a ruler-straight lakefront, an even street grid, O'Hare to the north-west.
f: In 1900 engineers reversed the Chicago River, sending it away from the lake towards the Mississippi.
The name comes from a local Native American word for a wild onion that grew along the river.
Most of Chicago's lakefront is kept as public parks and beaches rather than private land.

q.q: What did engineers do to the Chicago River in 1900?

Q1533.t: A valley city, walled off from the sea by one mountain
Q1533.s: Caracas stretches for some 20 km along a narrow valley about 900 m up, parallel to the Caribbean coast yet hidden from it. Between city and sea rises the green ridge of El Ávila, over 2,700 m at its highest. So the airport sits on the coast at Maiquetía, on the far side of the mountain. The city was founded in 1567.
Q1533.w: A long, narrow city in an east–west valley; a steep green ridge to the north, the blue sea just beyond it.
f: Simón Bolívar, who led much of South America to independence, was born in Caracas in 1783.
The city's full founding name was Santiago de León de Caracas.

q.q: What separates Caracas from the Caribbean Sea?

Q2868.t: A capital in the desert, under a lid of grey sea mist
Q2868.s: Lima is one of the driest capitals on Earth: a brown city on bare desert that gets barely a couple of centimetres of rain a year. Yet for months it hides under a low, grey sea fog, the garúa. Look for the cliffs where the city drops to the Pacific. Francisco Pizarro founded it in 1535 as the City of Kings.
Q2868.w: A vast tan city on a desert coast, edged by sea cliffs; bare brown hills inland and the green thread of the Rímac valley.
f: For more than two centuries Lima was the capital of a Spanish viceroyalty covering most of Spanish South America.
The port of Callao and the international airport lie just west of the centre, on the same coastal plain.
In winter the garúa can keep the sky grey for weeks while barely wetting the ground.

q.q: What did Pizarro name Lima when he founded it in 1535?

Q81033.t: An industrial city in a ring of jagged grey mountains
Q81033.s: Monterrey sits in a valley of the Sierra Madre Oriental, and the mountains crowd right up to its suburbs. The most famous is Cerro de la Silla, whose twin-humped ridge really does look like a saddle. Founded in 1596, the city became Mexico's industrial powerhouse: in 1900 the first large steelworks in Latin America was founded here.
Q81033.w: A dense city in a valley hemmed by steep, folded grey ridges; a saddle-shaped mountain on its eastern edge.
f: Cerro de la Silla rises to about 1,800 m, well over a kilometre above the city.
The Santa Catarina River that crosses the city is dry for most of the year.
The Huasteca Canyon on the western edge cuts deep into folded limestone ridges.

q.q: Which saddle-shaped mountain is the symbol of Monterrey?

Q24639.t: A green peninsula city between the inlet and the peaks
Q24639.s: Vancouver is all edges: sea on three sides, and snowy Coast Mountains rising almost straight from the northern shore. Look for the dark green thumb of Stanley Park pointing into Burrard Inlet, and the flat, chequered farmland of the Fraser delta to the south, where the airport sits on an island. The city was incorporated in 1886.
Q24639.w: A city on a peninsula between two waters; a dark green wooded tip, snowy peaks to the north, flat delta to the south.
f: Stanley Park covers about 400 hectares — more than New York's Central Park.
The inlet was charted in 1792 by Captain George Vancouver, whose name the city took.
The Canadian Pacific Railway arrived in 1887, making the city Canada's gateway to the Pacific.

q.q: Which river's delta lies on Vancouver's southern side?

Q172.t: A lakefront city with islands cupping its harbour
Q172.s: Toronto runs along the north shore of Lake Ontario, and the easiest way to spot it is a string of low green islands just offshore, curling round the harbour. Until a storm broke through in 1858 they were a sandy peninsula. Inland, look for deep wooded ravines snaking through the street grid. Until 1834 the town was called York.
Q172.w: A dense city on the north shore of Lake Ontario; a curl of low islands off downtown, green ravines inland.
f: One of the islands carries a small city airport, only a stone's throw from downtown.
The name is often traced to a Mohawk word for a place where trees stand in the water.
Toronto's network of wooded ravines is among the most extensive of any city in the world.

q.q: What was Toronto called before 1834?

Q1486.t: A grid of lights on a brown river as wide as a sea
Q1486.s: Buenos Aires faces the Río de la Plata, an estuary so broad that the Uruguayan shore lies roughly 50 km away, out of sight from the waterfront. The water is a milky coffee-brown, stained by silt from the Paraná and Uruguay rivers. Behind the shore, the city's square blocks march out across the flat pampas without a hill in sight.
Q1486.w: A vast grid city on the south bank of a wide brown estuary; the green maze of the Paraná Delta to the north-west.
f: The city was founded twice: first in 1536, then for good by Juan de Garay in 1580.
The Río de la Plata is formed where the Paraná and Uruguay rivers meet.
At night the regular blocks glow like an orange chessboard reaching far inland.

q.q: Who refounded Buenos Aires for good in 1580?

Q36091.t: A city of lakes, split by the young Mississippi
Q36091.s: Minneapolis is dotted with lakes, several of them strung together inside the city like blue beads. Through the middle runs the Mississippi, still a modest river here, dropping over St. Anthony Falls, the only natural major waterfall on its whole course. The falls powered the flour mills that, around 1900, made this the milling capital of the world.
Q36091.w: A flat city freckled with round lakes; the Mississippi winding through its centre and meeting the Minnesota River by the airport.
f: Minnesota has more than 11,000 lakes larger than 4 hectares — its '10,000 lakes' slogan undersells it.
St. Paul, the twin city and state capital, lies just downstream on the same river.
The airport sits right beside the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers.

q.q: Which industry made Minneapolis famous around 1900?

Q18094.t: A tropical city between a crater and green fluted ridges
Q18094.s: Honolulu is squeezed along Oʻahu's south shore, between the reef-fringed sea and the steep, fluted green ridges of the Koʻolau Range. At its eastern end rises Diamond Head, a crater so round it looks stamped into the coast. The nearest point of mainland North America is roughly 3,800 km away, which makes this one of the remotest big cities on Earth.
Q18094.w: A strip of city along an island's south coast; a round crater at the east end, a long runway on the water to the west.
f: Diamond Head is a volcanic tuff cone; sailors in the 1800s mistook glittering calcite crystals on its slopes for diamonds.
One of the airport's main runways, the Reef Runway, was built on landfill over a coral reef.
The name Honolulu is usually translated from Hawaiian as 'sheltered bay'.

q.q: What is Diamond Head in Honolulu?

Q5083.t: A city on a narrow neck of land, a giant volcano beyond
Q5083.s: Seattle sits on a slim strip of hilly land between the salt water of Puget Sound and the long, freshwater Lake Washington. On a clear day the view is stolen by Mount Rainier, a glacier-covered volcano of about 4,390 m some 90 km to the south-east. The city is named after Si'ahl, a leader of the local Duwamish and Suquamish peoples.
Q5083.w: A city between a fjord-like sound and a long lake; thin bridges floating across the lake; Rainier's white cone to the south-east.
f: The bridges over Lake Washington float on concrete pontoons; one is the world's longest floating bridge, about 2.3 km.
The Klondike gold rush of 1897 made Seattle the main outfitting port for prospectors heading north.
Mount Rainier carries more glacier ice than any other peak in the contiguous United States.

q.q: Which volcano looms south-east of Seattle?

Q16556.t: A mile-square grid stamped across the Sonoran Desert
Q16556.s: Phoenix is geometry on sand: a vast grid of arterial roads a mile apart, stamped across a desert valley and broken by bare rocky mountains. Watch for canals and green squares of irrigated land. Long before the city, the Hohokam people dug hundreds of kilometres of canals here, and settlers of the 1860s named their new town after the bird that rises from its ashes.
Q16556.w: A huge, pale, regular grid in brown desert, with dark rocky peaks poking through; thin canals and green irrigated patches.
f: The Hohokam canals, dug from about the 600s to the 1400s, formed one of the largest irrigation networks in pre-Columbian North America.
Summer afternoons here typically climb above 40 °C.
Camelback Mountain, surrounded by suburbs, is named for its hump-backed profile.

q.q: Why was Phoenix given its name?
q.a: It rose on the ruins of ancient canals

Q16552.t: A deep blue bay, a sandy spit and Mexico next door
Q16552.s: San Diego wraps around a long, sheltered bay, closed off from the Pacific by the flat Coronado peninsula and the high ridge of Point Loma. Planes land almost among the downtown towers, at an airport right on the water. Spanish friars founded California's first mission here in 1769, and the Mexican border is only about 25 km to the south.
Q16552.w: A curved bay behind a pale sandy spit and a long ridge; the city spreads over canyon-cut mesas, merging with Tijuana to the south.
f: In 1542 Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo sailed into this bay, the first European known to reach the US West Coast.
Coronado is not quite an island: a thin sand strip, the Silver Strand, ties it to the mainland.

q.q: What did Spanish friars found at San Diego in 1769?

Q38022.t: Where the muddy Missouri pours into the Mississippi
Q38022.s: Just north of St. Louis two of America's great rivers meet, and from above they often keep their colours for a while: the silt-laden Missouri alongside the darker Mississippi. French fur traders founded the town in 1764 and named it after King Louis IX. In 1804 Lewis and Clark set out from near the confluence to cross the continent.
Q38022.w: A city on the west bank of the Mississippi; to the north, two big brown rivers meet in a maze of channels and islands.
f: The Eads Bridge of 1874 was one of the first major bridges built with steel as its main material.
A little further upstream the Illinois River joins the Mississippi too.
The Gateway Arch on the riverfront is 192 m tall but far too slender to pick out from cruise.

q.q: Which river joins the Mississippi just north of St. Louis?

Q34404.t: The Crescent City, cradled in a bend of the Mississippi
Q34404.s: New Orleans grew inside a tight curve of the Mississippi, which is why it's called the Crescent City. To its north spreads the broad, round Lake Pontchartrain, crossed by a bridge nearly 40 km long — a hairline over the water. The French founded the city in 1718; much of it now lies below sea level, ringed by levees.
Q34404.w: A city in a sharp bend of a wide brown river; a big round lake to the north crossed by a hairline bridge.
f: The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, about 38 km long, is one of the longest bridges over water in the world.
The city is named after Philippe, Duke of Orléans, who ruled France as regent when it was founded.
In 1803 the United States bought New Orleans as part of the vast Louisiana Purchase.

q.q: Why is New Orleans called the Crescent City?
q.a: It sits in a bend of the Mississippi

Q16557.t: A prairie metropolis with an airport bigger than Manhattan
Q16557.s: Dallas rises from flat, open prairie, with no coast or mountain to give it shape — just freeways fanning out and a scatter of reservoirs. The Trinity River crosses it in a wide green floodway between levees. Towards Fort Worth, look for the runways of DFW, an airport that covers more ground than Manhattan. It all began with a trading post by a river ford in 1841.
Q16557.w: Flat sprawl without natural edges; a broad green floodway along the Trinity; a giant airport with long parallel runways to the north-west.
f: Dallas–Fort Worth International covers about 70 km², more than the island of Manhattan.
Founder John Neely Bryan picked the spot for its natural ford across the Trinity River.
Almost all the lakes around Dallas are man-made reservoirs.

q.q: Which river flows through Dallas?

Q171632.t: On the neck of a vast lake studded with oil wells
Q171632.s: Maracaibo sits on the narrow strait where Lake Maracaibo, one of South America's biggest bodies of water, opens to the sea. Out on the lake stand countless oil wells, and at night their lights speckle the dark water. Look for the thin line of the bridge across the strait, over 8 km long. In 1499 an expedition sailing for Spain saw stilt houses here and called the land 'Little Venice' — Venezuela.
Q171632.w: A city on the west shore of a narrow strait; a long bridge across it; a vast lake opening to the south.
f: Over the south-west of the lake, near the mouth of the Catatumbo River, lightning flickers on well over a hundred nights a year.
The General Rafael Urdaneta Bridge across the strait is about 8.7 km long and opened in 1962.
The lake is connected to the sea, so its water is slightly salty.

q.q: What gave Venezuela its name?

Q100.t: A city that built its own ground out into the harbour
Q100.s: Boston's outline is largely man-made. The Puritans who arrived in 1630 settled a small, hilly peninsula joined to the mainland by a thin neck; in the 1800s the mudflats around it were filled in to create whole districts. Look for the Charles River basin, the island-dotted harbour and the runways stretching into the sea just across from downtown.
Q100.w: A compact city on a harbour full of islands; a wide river basin to the west; runways reaching into the water to the east.
f: The Back Bay district stands on tidal flats that were filled in with gravel in the 1800s.
Harvard, founded in 1636 across the Charles River, is the oldest university in the United States.
Logan Airport was also built largely on land reclaimed from the harbour.

q.q: What was Boston's Back Bay before the 1800s?

Q49255.t: A city at the head of a bay stitched with causeways
Q49255.s: Tampa sits at the top of a big, branching bay, and from above the whole area looks stitched together: long causeways and bridges run straight across the shallow water to St. Petersburg on the peninsula opposite. In 1886 cigar makers moved their factories here, and hand-rolled cigars made Tampa famous. Look for the dredged shipping channel running out towards the Gulf.
Q49255.w: A city at the northern head of a wide, branching bay; several thin causeways across the water; a peninsula city to the west.
f: Tampa Bay is Florida's largest open-water estuary, covering about 1,000 km².
Ybor City, the old cigar district, once turned out hundreds of millions of cigars a year.

q.q: Which city faces Tampa across the bay?

Q1345.t: Penn's grid, laid out between two rivers in 1682
Q1345.s: Philadelphia began as a plan on paper: in 1682 William Penn drew a neat grid between the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers, with a central square and four smaller ones. That rectangle is still the heart of the city. The Declaration of Independence was adopted here in 1776, and for a decade from 1790 Philadelphia served as the nation's capital.
Q1345.w: A dense grid between two rivers; the wide Delaware to the east with the airport on its bank; a long green park along the Schuylkill.
f: Four of Penn's five original squares are still parks; the fifth holds City Hall.
The name is Greek for 'brotherly love'.
Fairmount Park, along the Schuylkill, is one of the largest urban park systems in the US.

q.q: Between which two rivers did Penn lay out Philadelphia?

Q12439.t: The US city with Canada to its south
Q12439.s: Detroit comes with a quirk of the map: across the Detroit River, due south of downtown, lies Canada. The river is really a strait linking Lake St. Clair to Lake Erie, and the French word for strait, détroit, gave the city its name. Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac founded a fort here in 1701. Two centuries later carmakers turned it into the Motor City.
Q12439.w: A city along a broad river channel between two lakes; Windsor on the opposite bank; a long wooded island in the river.
f: Belle Isle, the island park in the Detroit River, is larger than New York's Central Park.
The Ambassador Bridge to Windsor carries more trade than any other US–Canada border crossing.

q.q: In which direction from downtown Detroit does Canada lie?

Q39450.t: A frontier city between mudflats and the Chugach peaks
Q39450.s: Anchorage fills a wedge of flat land between two long arms of Cook Inlet, with the Chugach Mountains rising right behind it. At low tide the inlet drains to glistening grey mudflats: the tides here can rise and fall by more than 9 m. On a clear day, look north for Denali, about 200 km away. The city began in 1914 as a tent camp for railway builders.
Q39450.w: A grid city on a lowland wedge between two grey-brown inlets, backed by snowy mountains; a lake full of floatplanes beside the airport.
f: Lake Hood, next to the international airport, is one of the world's busiest seaplane bases.
Turnagain Arm got its name in 1778, when James Cook's ships had to turn back there.
In Turnagain Arm the incoming tide sometimes arrives as a bore — a single travelling wave.

q.q: How did Turnagain Arm near Anchorage get its name?
q.a: Cook's ships had to turn back there
x: Whalers used it as a turning point

Q9022.t: Between a deep canyon and Mexico's largest lake
Q9022.s: Guadalajara spreads across a high, open valley about 1,560 m above sea level. Its northern edge ends abruptly at a deep canyon cut by the Río Grande de Santiago, and to the south lies Lake Chapala, Mexico's largest freshwater lake. West of the city, look for blue-grey rows of agave: this is the country around the town of Tequila.
Q9022.w: A large city on a flat high valley; a dark canyon along its northern edge; a big lake to the south.
f: The canyon at the northern edge, the Barranca de Huentitán, is roughly 600 m deep.
The city was moved several times before settling on its present site in 1542.
Blue agave for tequila covers the hills around the town of Tequila, about 60 km north-west.

q.q: Which lake lies just south of Guadalajara?

Q125293.t: A colonial grid ringed by great volcanoes
Q125293.s: Few cities have a volcanic horizon like Puebla's. To the west stand snowy Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl, to the north-east the lone cone of La Malinche, and far to the east the white peak of Orizaba, Mexico's highest mountain. The Spanish founded Puebla in 1531 as a brand-new planned town, and its old centre is still a tidy grid.
Q125293.w: A large city on a high plain with big volcanoes on the horizon; La Malinche's isolated cone close by to the north-east.
f: Next door in Cholula stands the largest pyramid in the world by volume, so overgrown it looks like a hill.
Pico de Orizaba, visible to the east on clear days, rises to about 5,600 m.
Puebla is famous for Talavera, a glazed pottery tradition brought from Spain in the 1500s.

q.q: Which nearby town has the largest pyramid in the world by volume?

Q43509.t: A tidal river port among mangroves and shrimp ponds
Q43509.s: Guayaquil spreads along the west bank of the broad, brown Guayas River, where the Pacific tide still reaches. Downstream the estuary dissolves into a maze of mangrove channels and neat grids of rectangular shrimp ponds. Ecuador's biggest city and main port, it was founded on this spot in 1538, after earlier attempts nearby.
Q43509.w: A large city beside a wide brown river; rows of rectangular ponds and dark mangroves along the estuary to the south.
f: The ponds around the Gulf of Guayaquil help make Ecuador one of the world's biggest shrimp exporters.
Rafts of floating water hyacinth drift up and down the Guayas with every tide.
Francisco de Orellana, later the first European to sail down the Amazon, is credited with the 1538 founding.

q.q: Which river flows past Guayaquil?

Q48278.t: A city filling a green Andean valley from wall to wall
Q48278.s: Medellín is poured into the Aburrá Valley, a narrow trough in the Andes about 1,500 m up, and its red-brick neighbourhoods climb high up both slopes. Down the middle runs the Medellín River, heading north. At this height and so close to the equator the air stays mild all year, which is why locals call it the City of Eternal Spring.
Q48278.w: A long city in a narrow north–south valley, climbing its green walls; the main airport on a plateau to the east.
f: The main airport stands on a plateau near Rionegro, at about 2,100 m — higher than the city itself.
The average temperature stays around 22 °C in every month of the year.
Medellín was granted the status of a town in 1675.

q.q: What is Medellín's nickname, thanks to its climate?

Q51103.t: Salsa city on a plain of sugar cane
Q51103.s: Cali sits where the flat, fertile Cauca Valley meets the steep green slopes of the Western Andes. Look out across the valley floor: a patchwork of sugar cane fields in every shade of green stretches north and south for well over a hundred kilometres. Sebastián de Belalcázar founded the city in 1536; today it proudly calls itself the world capital of salsa.
Q51103.w: A large city at the foot of a mountain wall to the west; a flat valley of striped green cane fields to the east.
f: The Cauca Valley is the heart of Colombia's sugar industry.
The Cauca River, one of Colombia's longest, winds along the city's eastern edge.
At about 1,000 m, Cali is lower and warmer than Colombia's highland cities.

q.q: Which crop blankets the Cauca Valley around Cali?

Q1563.t: A pocket harbour behind a narrow, fortified mouth
Q1563.s: Havana grew around a bag-shaped bay entered through a single narrow channel, easy to defend and safe from storms. That made it the gathering point for Spain's treasure fleets, which assembled here before crossing the Atlantic. The city moved to this shore in 1519. Look for the harbour's slim neck and the long seafront curving west from it.
Q1563.w: A city on Cuba's north coast around a pouch-shaped bay with a slender entrance; the old town on its western side.
f: Old Havana and its fortifications have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1982.
Key West, in Florida, lies about 170 km to the north across the Straits of Florida.
The Morro and La Cabaña fortresses guard the harbour mouth from its eastern shore.

q.q: What gathered in Havana harbour before crossing to Spain?

Q34820.t: The Americas' oldest European city, at a river mouth
Q34820.s: Santo Domingo lies where the Ozama River meets the Caribbean, and its colonial quarter sits on the west bank right at the river mouth. Founded in 1496, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the Americas. Look for the long, straight seafront running west from the river, and the airport out on the coast to the east.
Q34820.w: A large city along a straight stretch of Caribbean coast, split by a river mouth; the airport on the coast to the east.
f: In 1502 the city moved from the east bank of the Ozama to the west bank.
Its cathedral, completed in the 1540s, is the oldest in the Americas.

q.q: Which river splits Santo Domingo into west and east?

Q12829733.t: A river port at the gates of the Amazon
Q12829733.s: Belém faces a vast expanse of muddy water — the Pará River and Guajará Bay, part of the Amazon's maze of mouths. Across it lies Marajó, an island roughly the size of Switzerland. The Portuguese built a fort here in 1616 to guard the way into the Amazon, and the rubber boom of the late 1800s made the city rich.
Q12829733.w: A dense city on a point between brown waterways, forest and islands all around; the huge, low island of Marajó to the north-west.
f: Marajó covers about 40,000 km², one of the largest islands ringed by fresh and brackish water.
Belém lies less than 200 km south of the equator, and afternoon downpours are almost daily.
The Ver-o-Peso waterfront market has traded Amazon goods since the 1600s.

q.q: Which huge island lies across the water from Belém?

Q2844.t: A capital drawn in the shape of an aeroplane
Q2844.s: Brasília is one of the few cities whose design you can read from the window: two curved residential wings crossed by a straight monumental axis, like an aeroplane or a bird. Lúcio Costa drew the plan, and the city was built on almost empty savanna and inaugurated in 1960. An artificial lake wraps around it on the east.
Q2844.w: A cross-shaped city — a long straight axis across a curved arc — beside a branching man-made lake on the high savanna.
f: Lake Paranoá was created by damming a river when the city was built.
The whole Pilot Plan has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1987.
The city stands on a plateau at about 1,100 m, amid Brazil's reddish cerrado savanna.

q.q: What does Brasília's original plan resemble?

Q40269.t: A city on a river that might be a lake
Q40269.s: Porto Alegre lines the eastern shore of the Guaíba, a broad body of water formed where several rivers meet in a green delta of islands. Locals still argue whether it counts as a river or a lake. To the south it opens into the Lagoa dos Patos, a coastal lagoon more than 200 km long. Settlers from the Azores helped found the town in the 1700s.
Q40269.w: A city on the east bank of wide brown water; a delta of green islands to the north, a vast lagoon to the south.
f: The Lagoa dos Patos covers about 10,000 km², making it Brazil's largest lagoon.
The official founding date is 1772, though Azorean families had settled here some twenty years earlier.

q.q: Which lagoon stretches away south of Porto Alegre?

Q4361.t: A cool plateau city among candelabra pines
Q4361.s: Curitiba sits on a high plateau about 900 m up, just inland from the forested Serra do Mar, and is one of Brazil's coolest big cities, with frosty winter mornings. Its name is usually traced to a Tupi phrase for 'many pines', after the araucaria trees whose flat, candelabra crowns still dot the countryside. Look for the lakes in its many parks.
Q4361.w: A large city on a green plateau dotted with park lakes; the dark, forested Serra do Mar rising to the east.
f: Many of the city's park lakes were created as flood-control reservoirs.
A railway opened in 1885 still winds down the Serra do Mar from Curitiba to the port of Paranaguá.
In the 1970s Curitiba pioneered express bus lanes that cities around the world later copied.

q.q: Which tree gave Curitiba its name?

Q43463.t: A sunny fortress city on Brazil's north-east shoulder
Q43463.s: Fortaleza faces north onto a warm, turquoise Atlantic, its high-rise seafront curving along a coast of white dunes. The steady trade winds that fill the sails of local jangada rafts also turn rows of wind turbines along the shore. The name simply means 'fortress': the city grew around a fort the Dutch built here in 1649, later taken over by the Portuguese.
Q43463.w: A large city on a north-facing coast; long pale beaches and dunes on either side; breakwaters and a port at its eastern end.
f: Ceará, the state Fortaleza is capital of, abolished slavery in 1884, four years before the rest of Brazil.
The coast here lies only about 4° south of the equator, so days and nights stay nearly equal all year.

q.q: What does the name Fortaleza mean?

Q36947.t: Brazil's first capital, on a cliff above All Saints Bay
Q36947.s: Salvador occupies a blunt peninsula between the open Atlantic and the huge, calm Bay of All Saints. Its old town was built on top of a steep escarpment, with the port crowded at the foot — a city on two levels. Founded in 1549, it served as the capital of Portuguese Brazil for more than two centuries, until 1763.
Q36947.w: A big city on a triangular peninsula; a wide, island-studded bay to the west, ocean beaches to the south and east.
f: The bay was named in 1501 by a Portuguese expedition that arrived on All Saints' Day.
Since 1873 a public lift, the Lacerda Elevator, has carried people between the upper and lower towns.
The bay covers more than 1,000 km² and holds dozens of islands.

q.q: Which bay did Salvador grow up beside?

Q2096.t: A green river gorge winding through a northern city
Q2096.s: Edmonton is cut in two by the North Saskatchewan River, which loops through a deep, wooded valley kept almost entirely as parkland. From above it's a dark green ribbon across the grid of streets. Around the city, flat farmland stretches to the horizon. This is the northernmost metropolis of more than a million people in North America.
Q2096.w: A large grid city on flat farmland, split by a deep, winding, tree-lined river valley; refineries on the eastern edge.
f: The river valley parks form one of the longest continuous stretches of urban parkland in North America.
The Hudson's Bay Company built Fort Edmonton on the river in 1795.
Edmonton is Alberta's capital, though Calgary to the south is the larger city.

q.q: Which river winds through Edmonton?

Q340.t: An island city with a mountain at its heart
Q340.s: Montreal fills most of an island in the St. Lawrence, and in its middle rises a dark, wooded hill: Mount Royal, which gave the city its name. Jacques Cartier climbed it in 1535, and in 1642 French settlers founded Ville-Marie below. Just upstream the Lachine Rapids stopped ocean-going ships, so the city grew into a great river port.
Q340.w: A large island city in a broad river, with a wooded hill in the middle; long bridges to the south shore.
f: The island of Montreal, about 50 km long, is the largest of more than 200 islands in the Hochelaga Archipelago.
Ships now bypass the Lachine Rapids through the St. Lawrence Seaway along the south shore.
Montreal is one of the largest French-speaking cities in the world.

q.q: What is Montreal named after?

Q83189.t: A 1930s planned capital on the red cerrado plateau
Q83189.s: Goiânia was drawn on a drawing board and built from 1933 to replace the old colonial town of Goiás as state capital. Its central avenues radiate from a civic square like spokes, a plan a generation older than Brasília's. Around it the cerrado savanna has become a patchwork of soy fields and pasture, with reddish soil showing between them.
Q83189.w: A large city on a gently rolling plateau; green and red-brown squares of farmland all round; Brasília about 200 km to the north-east.
f: The old capital, the town of Goiás, is a UNESCO World Heritage site for its colonial centre.
Many of Goiânia's early public buildings were built in Art Deco style.

q.q: Which town did Goiânia replace as state capital?

Q48344.t: A city of rivers and bridges behind a natural reef
Q48344.s: Recife is threaded with water: the Capibaribe and Beberibe rivers split into channels around islands before reaching the sea, and bridges stitch the districts together. Offshore, a long, straight line of rock runs parallel to the beach and shelters the harbour — the reef that gave the city its name. From 1630 to 1654 this was the capital of Dutch Brazil.
Q48344.w: A dense coastal city criss-crossed by river channels; a thin line of reef just offshore; a long beach to the south.
f: The first synagogue in the Americas, Kahal Zur Israel, opened here in the 1630s under Dutch rule.
Under Johan Maurits of Nassau the Dutch built a new town, Mauritsstad, on one of the islands.

q.q: What does the name Recife mean?

Q49219.t: A city planned from scratch on an old cattle ranch
Q49219.s: Irvine was drawn up almost from nothing in the 1960s on the Irvine Ranch, once a huge cattle and farming estate stretching from the coast to the mountains. Architect William Pereira laid it out around a new University of California campus, in tidy villages divided by green belts. To the north-east, look for Saddleback, the twin-peaked ridge that shapes the skyline.
Q49219.w: Tidy curving suburbs with green belts, between low coastal hills and the Santa Ana Mountains; John Wayne Airport on the western edge.
f: Saddleback is named for the dip between its two summits; the higher one, Santiago Peak, is about 1,700 m.
Departures from John Wayne Airport climb steeply and throttle back to spare the houses below.
Upper Newport Bay, just to the south-west, is one of southern California's few surviving coastal estuaries.

q.q: What was the land under Irvine before the city was planned?

Q42800.t: A planned capital walled in by iron-rich mountains
Q42800.s: Belo Horizonte was built from scratch and inaugurated in 1897 as the new capital of Minas Gerais, replacing the old gold town of Ouro Preto. Its planners overlaid a street grid with diagonal avenues, all wrapped in a ring road. Along the southern edge rises the Serra do Curral, and beyond it lie the red-brown scars of iron-ore mines. The name means 'beautiful horizon'.
Q42800.w: A big, hilly city under a long ridge to the south; reddish mine pits in the hills beyond; a lake on the northern side.
f: The surrounding 'Iron Quadrangle' is one of the world's great iron-ore regions.
Lake Pampulha, an artificial lake in the north, is ringed by 1940s buildings by Oscar Niemeyer, now UNESCO-listed.

q.q: Which old gold town did Belo Horizonte replace as capital in 1897?

Q1335.t: The southernmost capital in the Americas, by a lone hill
Q1335.s: Montevideo sits on a rocky peninsula on the north shore of the Río de la Plata, just where the brown estuary begins to turn into the blue Atlantic. Across its bay rises a lone, rounded hill, the Cerro, which gave the city its name. Spain founded Montevideo in the 1720s as a fortress to hold the estuary's north shore against Portugal.
Q1335.w: A city on a peninsula and a long curving shore; a round hill across the bay to the west; brown water shading to blue eastward.
f: The Cerro de Montevideo is only about 134 m high, but it was the landmark sailors steered by.
Montevideo is the southernmost national capital in the Americas.
A seaside promenade, the Rambla, follows the shore for more than 20 km.

q.q: What gave Montevideo its name?

Q38733.t: A gold-rush capital at the edge of the Rockies
Q38733.s: Helena began in 1864, when four worn-out prospectors tried one last creek and struck gold; the town's main street still follows that 'Last Chance Gulch'. Today it's a small state capital where forested mountains meet the flat, open Helena Valley. Look for the Missouri River's reservoirs glinting to the north-east and east.
Q38733.w: A small town tucked against wooded hills; a broad, flat valley to the north-east, with the Missouri's blue reservoirs beyond.
f: In 1805 Meriwether Lewis named a narrow canyon of the Missouri nearby the 'Gates of the Rocky Mountains'.
Helena became Montana's capital in 1875, while Montana was still a territory.

q.q: What was the gulch called where Helena's gold was found?

Q37066.t: A prairie capital named to charm German investors
Q37066.s: Bismarck lies on the east bank of the Missouri, here a wide river winding through open, rolling plains. The town began in 1872 as Edwinton, a railway crossing; a year later it was renamed after Germany's chancellor, Otto von Bismarck, in the hope of drawing German money and settlers to the Northern Pacific Railway. Its twin town, Mandan, faces it across the river.
Q37066.w: A modest city on a broad, winding river with sandbars; a smaller town across the water; wide tan prairie all around.
f: Lewis and Clark spent the winter of 1804–05 at Fort Mandan, about 60 km up the river.
North Dakota's capitol is a 19-storey tower, often called the 'Skyscraper on the Prairie'.

q.q: Who is Bismarck named after?

Q35775.t: A green river of trees across the sagebrush
Q35775.s: From above, Boise's origin story makes sense: a ribbon of cottonwoods follows the Boise River out of the mountains and across a dry, sage-grey plain. French-Canadian fur trappers are said to have greeted the trees with 'Les bois!', and the name stuck. Today the city spreads from the foothills onto the irrigated patchwork of the Snake River Plain.
Q35775.w: A city at the foot of bare brown foothills; a green, tree-lined river running west through it onto a patchwork of farmland.
f: Idaho's capitol is the only US state capitol heated by water from underground hot springs.
Boise has one of the largest Basque communities in the United States.

q.q: Where does the name Boise come from?

Q16553.t: The flat heart of Silicon Valley, once all orchards
Q16553.s: San Jose spreads across the flat floor of the Santa Clara Valley, between the wooded Santa Cruz Mountains to the west and the bare, rounded Diablo Range to the east. Founded in 1777, it was the first Spanish civilian town in California. Until the mid-1900s the valley was a sea of fruit orchards; now it's the hub of Silicon Valley.
Q16553.w: A vast, low city on a flat valley floor at the southern tip of San Francisco Bay; mountains on both sides.
f: San Jose was California's first state capital, from 1849 to 1851.
On Mount Hamilton to the east, Lick Observatory opened in 1888, one of the first mountaintop observatories.

q.q: What was the Santa Clara Valley known for before computers?

Q18013.t: A gold-rush capital where two rivers meet
Q18013.s: Sacramento sits where the American River flows into the Sacramento, in the middle of California's flat Central Valley. In 1848 gold was found at a sawmill up the American River, and this riverside settlement became the supply town for the rush. Look west for a wide, straight belt of fields between levees: the Yolo Bypass, which floods on purpose in wet winters.
Q18013.w: A tree-filled city at a river junction on a flat valley floor; rice paddies around; a broad, leveed flood channel to the west.
f: In spring the flooded rice fields around the city can shine like mirrors.
The Central Pacific began building the first transcontinental railway eastward from Sacramento in 1863.
Sacramento has been California's capital since 1854.

q.q: Which river flows into the Sacramento River in the city?

Q23768.t: A blaze of light in a black desert
Q23768.s: At night Las Vegas is unmistakable: a dense pool of white and gold light in a desert that's otherwise almost completely dark, with one brilliant stripe running north–south through it. By day the valley shows its bones — bare mountains all round, snow on Mount Charleston in winter. The name is Spanish for 'the meadows', after springs that once watered grass here.
Q23768.w: A sharply bounded city in a desert basin ringed by bare mountains; the blue of Lake Mead about 40 km to the east.
f: The city was founded in 1905 with a railway company's auction of town lots.
Lake Mead, formed by the Hoover Dam, is the largest reservoir in the US by capacity.
Mount Charleston, west of the city, rises to about 3,630 m.

q.q: What does 'Las Vegas' mean in Spanish?

Q38555.t: America's oldest and highest state capital
Q38555.s: Santa Fe is easy to miss: a low, earth-coloured town of adobe walls that blends into the piñon-dotted hills at the foot of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. Spanish colonists founded it around 1610, making it the oldest state capital in the US, and at about 2,100 m it is also the highest. The broad Rio Grande valley opens to the west.
Q38555.w: A small, low, tan town at the southern tip of a snowy range; dark green juniper hills around; a wide valley to the west.
f: The Santa Fe Trail, opened in 1821, linked the town to Missouri by a trade route of well over 1,000 km.
The name Sangre de Cristo ('Blood of Christ') is often linked to the mountains' red glow at sunset.
The Palace of the Governors, built in the 1610s, is among the oldest public buildings in the US.

q.q: When was Santa Fe founded?

Q6106.t: A city of bridges under the white cone of Mount Hood
Q6106.s: Portland straddles the Willamette River just before it joins the broad Columbia, and a string of bridges stitches its two halves together. On a clear day Mount Hood's snowy cone floats on the eastern horizon. The name was settled in 1845 by a coin toss: one founder wanted Boston, the other Portland, after his home town in Maine.
Q6106.w: A city on both banks of a river just above a much wider one; a dark wooded ridge to the west; Mount Hood east.
f: Forest Park, on the ridge above the city, is one of the largest urban forests in the United States.
Mount Hood, about 3,430 m high, is a volcano and Oregon's highest peak.
The Columbia River here forms the border between Oregon and Washington.

q.q: How was Portland's name chosen in 1845?

Q23337.t: A grid city between a mountain wall and a salty inland sea
Q23337.s: Salt Lake City sits on a flat bench between the abrupt wall of the Wasatch Range and the shallow, glittering Great Salt Lake. Look at the lower mountain slopes for faint horizontal lines: old shorelines of Lake Bonneville, the vast ancient lake of which the Great Salt Lake is a remnant. Mormon pioneers founded the city in 1847 and laid out its grid of very wide streets.
Q23337.w: A city at the foot of a steep mountain wall; a vast pale lake to the north-west, with colourful evaporation ponds along its shore.
f: A railway causeway splits the lake, and the saltier northern part often looks pinkish-red from above.
Street addresses count outward from a single central point, Temple Square.
In places the Great Salt Lake is several times saltier than the ocean.

q.q: Which ancient lake left terraces on the mountains around Salt Lake City?

Q39042.t: A railway town that sprang up on the windy high plains
Q39042.s: Cheyenne stands alone on open high plains about 1,850 m up, with the low, pine-dark Laramie Range to the west. It was born in 1867, when the Union Pacific tracks arrived, and grew so fast it was nicknamed the Magic City of the Plains. Look for the railway running east–west through town: the reason it exists at all.
Q39042.w: A compact town on bare, rolling grassland; a railway line straight through it; low, dark hills to the west.
f: In 1869 the territorial legislature in Cheyenne gave women the vote — a first in the United States.
Cheyenne Frontier Days, held every July since 1897, is one of the world's largest outdoor rodeos.

q.q: What did Wyoming's legislature in Cheyenne grant first in 1869?

Q39709.t: A capital at a river fork in a sea of corn
Q39709.s: Des Moines grew where the Raccoon River flows into the Des Moines, and from above it sits like a knot in a vast chequerboard: Iowa's fields, laid out in one-mile squares of corn and soybeans, run to every horizon. The US Army founded Fort Des Moines at the fork in 1843. Look north for the long reservoir of Saylorville Lake.
Q39709.w: A mid-sized city at a river junction, surrounded by a perfect grid of square fields; a long, narrow lake to the north.
f: The name comes from the river's French name, often translated as 'River of the Monks', though its origin is debated.
Iowa was surveyed into square miles in the 1800s, and its country roads still follow that grid.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Des Moines?
q.a: The Des Moines and the Raccoon

Q43199.t: A river city where the Missouri once switched sides
Q43199.s: Omaha lines the west bank of the Missouri, a brown river looping across a wide floodplain, with Council Bluffs in Iowa on the other side. Look by the airport for a horseshoe-shaped lake: it's an old river bend, cut off when the Missouri changed course in 1877. The town beside it stayed in Iowa, stranded on the Nebraska bank.
Q43199.w: A city on bluffs above a winding brown river; a horseshoe lake and the airport on the floodplain; Council Bluffs across the water.
f: In the 1860s the Union Pacific began building the first transcontinental railway westward from Omaha.
The city, founded in 1854, is named after the Omaha people.
Carter Lake is the only Iowa town west of the Missouri River.

q.q: Why is Carter Lake, Iowa, on Omaha's side of the Missouri?

Q34863.t: A city that appeared in a single afternoon in 1889
Q34863.s: Oklahoma City has an unusual birthday. At noon on 22 April 1889 a gunshot opened the Land Run, and settlers raced in to claim plots; by nightfall around 10,000 people were camped on what had been open prairie. Today the city sprawls across flat, reddish plains, with round reservoirs on its edges and the Oklahoma River running through.
Q34863.w: A very spread-out city on flat red-brown plains; round blue reservoirs to the north-west; a river channel just south of downtown.
f: Oil wells have pumped on the grounds of the State Capitol — a sign of the oil field beneath the city.
Oklahoma City covers about 1,600 km², making it one of the largest US cities by land area.

q.q: How did Oklahoma City come into being in 1889?

Q40747.t: A tiny capital below a dam and a 370-km lake
Q40747.s: Pierre, pronounced 'peer', is one of the smallest state capitals in the US, a quiet town on the Missouri amid treeless, rolling plains. Just upstream the river is blocked by Oahe Dam, a huge earthen embankment, and behind it Lake Oahe winds north for some 370 km, almost to Bismarck, the capital of North Dakota.
Q40747.w: A small town on a river just below a massive earth dam; a long, winding blue lake stretching north through bare brown hills.
f: In 1743 French explorers buried a lead plate claiming the land for France on a hill across the river; children found it in 1913.
The town is named after Pierre Chouteau Jr., a fur trader based in St. Louis.

q.q: Which huge reservoir begins just north of Pierre?

Q975.t: Where the Texas Hill Country drops to the plains
Q975.s: San Antonio sits right on the Balcones Escarpment, and from above you can see the change: rumpled, wooded hills to the north-west, flat, open farmland to the south-east. Spanish missionaries and soldiers founded the settlement in 1718 by the springs of the San Antonio River. A chain of five missions along the river, the Alamo among them, is now a World Heritage site.
Q975.w: A big, sprawling city where dark green hills to the north-west meet flat plains to the south-east; freeway rings around the centre.
f: In 2015 the San Antonio Missions became the first UNESCO World Heritage site in Texas.
Much of the city's water comes from the Edwards Aquifer, a vast limestone reservoir beneath the escarpment.

q.q: When was San Antonio founded?

Q820235.t: An Andean terrace city near the Colombian border
Q820235.s: San Cristóbal sits on a series of terraces above the Torbes River, about 800 m up, in a green valley where Venezuela's Andes begin. The mountains here form a knot between the Colombian ranges to the south-west and the high Cordillera de Mérida to the north-east. Captain Juan Maldonado founded the city in 1561; Venezuelans know it as the City of Courtesy.
Q820235.w: A city spread over stepped terraces in a green mountain valley; forested ridges all round; a river winding along the valley floor.
f: The border with Colombia runs only a few dozen kilometres to the west, near the city of Cúcuta.
To the north-east the Andes climb to Pico Bolívar, Venezuela's highest peak, at about 4,980 m.

q.q: What do Venezuelans call San Cristóbal?

Q54880.t: An industrial city beside a lake with no way to the sea
Q54880.s: Valencia spreads over a green valley beside Lake Valencia, a broad lake ringed by mountains with no outlet to the sea. When Alexander von Humboldt came here in 1800, he noticed that the water had been falling and blamed the clearing of forests around it — one of the earliest scientific warnings about human impact on nature. The city itself was founded in 1555.
Q54880.w: A large city in a flat valley west of a wide lake; the forested Coastal Range to the north, the sea just beyond it.
f: Lake Valencia is Venezuela's largest natural freshwater lake.
The port of Puerto Cabello lies about 35 km to the north, on the far side of the coastal mountains.

q.q: Who studied Lake Valencia's falling water level in 1800?

Q28198.t: A capital on the Pearl River, above a buried volcano
Q28198.s: Jackson lies on gently rolling, wooded land beside the Pearl River, with the broad Ross Barnett Reservoir glinting to the north-east. Nothing at the surface hints at it, but about 900 m underground lies an extinct volcano, long buried by sediment. The site began as a trading post called LeFleur's Bluff and was chosen as the state capital in 1821, named after Andrew Jackson.
Q28198.w: A mid-sized city in green, rolling woodland; a winding river on its east side; a large reservoir to the north-east.
f: The buried Jackson Volcano was last active tens of millions of years ago, in the age of the dinosaurs.
The Natchez Trace, an old trail of traders and travellers, passes nearby as a scenic parkway.

q.q: What lies buried deep beneath Jackson?

Q41087.t: The City of Oaks, a capital planned in a forest
Q41087.s: Raleigh hides under trees: from above, rooftops and roads peek through an almost continuous canopy of oak and pine. It was planned from scratch in 1792, when North Carolina bought land in the woods for a new capital, and named after Sir Walter Raleigh, sponsor of the Roanoke colony. Look for the branching reservoirs of Falls Lake and Jordan Lake nearby.
Q41087.w: A city deep in green forest; a compact downtown; branching reservoirs to the north and west; the airport among trees to the north-west.
f: Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill form the 'Research Triangle', with a large research park between them.
The 1792 plan put the State House on a central square, with four smaller squares around it.

q.q: Who is Raleigh named after?

Q37320.t: A lake port where a crooked river meets Lake Erie
Q37320.s: Cleveland spreads along the south shore of Lake Erie, and its heart is where the Cuyahoga River winds through a valley of old industry before slipping into the lake. The name Cuyahoga is often translated as 'crooked river', and from above it's easy to see why. Surveyor Moses Cleaveland laid out the town in 1796; the city later dropped the first 'a'.
Q37320.w: A city along a straight lakeshore; a tightly winding river through the centre; a small airport right on the waterfront.
f: Cuyahoga Valley, just south of the city, is Ohio's only national park.
Burke Lakefront Airport sits on land reclaimed from Lake Erie, next to downtown.

q.q: Who laid out Cleveland in 1796?

Q43196.t: A hilly river city whose airport is in another state
Q43196.s: Cincinnati fills a bowl of hills on the north bank of the Ohio River, which swings past in broad curves; across the water is Kentucky. The city's main airport is on the Kentucky side too. Founded in 1788, it was named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which honoured Cincinnatus, the Roman statesman who went back to his plough after saving Rome.
Q43196.w: A city in green hills along a curving river; towns on the opposite, Kentucky bank; a big airport on the plateau to the south-west.
f: The Roebling Suspension Bridge, finished in 1866, was a forerunner of the same engineer's Brooklyn Bridge.
In the 1800s the city packed so much pork that it was nicknamed Porkopolis.

q.q: In which state is Cincinnati's main airport?

Q23197.t: Music City in the loops of the Cumberland River
Q23197.s: Nashville grew on the bluffs of the Cumberland River, which coils through the city in wide, lazy loops before heading north. Settlers built Fort Nashborough here in 1779. Look for the reservoirs east of town, Percy Priest and Old Hickory, their arms reaching into wooded hills. The nickname Music City comes from its country-music studios and radio stages.
Q23197.w: A city in rolling green country, with a winding river making big loops through it; branching lakes to the east and north-east.
f: The Grand Ole Opry has broadcast from Nashville every week since 1925, the longest-running radio show in the US.
The city was named after Francis Nash, a general from North Carolina.

q.q: Which river loops through Nashville?

Q16563.t: A bluff-top river city named after Egypt's ancient capital
Q16563.s: Memphis sits on bluffs on the east bank of the Mississippi, above the river's floods; across the water the Arkansas side is flat floodplain scattered with curved oxbow lakes. Its founders in 1819 likened the river to the Nile and named the town after the ancient Egyptian capital. At night its airport is famously busy: it's the main hub of a giant cargo airline.
Q16563.w: A city on high ground on the east bank of a broad, winding brown river; flat farmland and oxbow lakes on the Arkansas side.
f: For years Memphis was the world's busiest cargo airport, thanks to FedEx's overnight hub.
The two steel arches of the Hernando de Soto Bridge over the river form the letter 'M'.

q.q: Which state lies across the Mississippi from Memphis?

Q49231.t: A harbour city at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay
Q49231.s: Norfolk sits on Hampton Roads, a great natural anchorage where several rivers pour into the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. Look east across the bay entrance for a thin line that suddenly vanishes: the Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel, which dives under the shipping lanes between man-made islands. South of the city stretches the dark forest of the Great Dismal Swamp.
Q49231.w: A low, watery city of peninsulas and inlets on a vast harbour; a long causeway crossing the bay mouth to the north-east.
f: The Bridge–Tunnel, opened in 1964, runs about 28 km from shore to shore, with two tunnels under the channels.
Lake Drummond, in the middle of the Great Dismal Swamp, is one of only two natural lakes in Virginia.
Hampton Roads is one of the largest natural harbours in the world.

q.q: What links the two shores at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay?

Q37836.t: Three rivers, three rival towns and a Great Lake
Q37836.s: Milwaukee sits where three rivers join and flow into Lake Michigan behind a long breakwater. Each river bank once belonged to a rival settlement, and when the three merged in 1846 their street grids didn't match — which is why several bridges still cross the river at an angle. German immigrants later made the city famous for its beer.
Q37836.w: A city on the western shore of Lake Michigan, where three rivers meet in a harbour sheltered by long breakwaters.
f: In the late 1800s some of America's biggest breweries were based in Milwaukee.
The opposite, Michigan shore of the lake lies about 130 km away.

q.q: How many rival settlements merged to form Milwaukee in 1846?

Q40435.t: Where Lake Erie pours into the Niagara River
Q40435.s: Buffalo stands at the eastern tip of Lake Erie, right where the lake drains into the Niagara River and starts its run north to the falls, about 30 km away. In 1825 the Erie Canal linked this spot to the Hudson and New York, and Buffalo boomed as the gateway to the Great Lakes. In winter, look for bands of lake-effect snow.
Q40435.w: A city at the eastern corner of Lake Erie; a river flowing north from it along the Canadian border towards Niagara Falls.
f: The world's first steam-powered grain elevator was built here in 1842.
Wind blowing over the unfrozen lake can dump snow on the city in narrow, very intense bands.
The Peace Bridge links Buffalo with Fort Erie, in Canada, at the head of the river.

q.q: Which canal ended at Buffalo when it opened in 1825?

Q1342.t: Where two rivers meet to begin the Ohio
Q1342.s: Pittsburgh's downtown is a sharp triangle of land where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet to form the Ohio, and from above that point stands out clearly. All around, the rivers run through steep, wooded valleys crossed by bridge after bridge. In 1758 the British named the spot after the statesman William Pitt and soon built Fort Pitt at the point.
Q1342.w: A pointed wedge of towers where two rivers merge into one; hills and deep river valleys all around, crossed by many bridges.
f: Pittsburgh has around 450 bridges, often said to be more than any other city in the world.
For much of the 20th century the city was the heart of American steelmaking.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Pittsburgh to form the Ohio?

Q507080.t: A planned city where dark water meets muddy water
Q507080.s: Look where two great rivers meet: the Caroní, dark as strong tea, flows into the broad, muddy Orinoco, and the two colours run side by side before blending. Ciudad Guayana spreads over both banks of the Caroní, a city planned in 1961 by merging two older towns, Puerto Ordaz and San Félix. Its steel and aluminium plants run on power from dams upstream.
Q507080.w: A city on both sides of a dark river where it joins a much wider, pale brown one; industrial plants along the shore.
f: The Caroní's dark colour comes from tannins washed out of forest soils.
The Guri Dam, upstream on the Caroní, is one of the largest hydroelectric plants in the world.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Ciudad Guayana?

Q79985.t: Russian America's first capital, on a big green island
Q79985.s: Kodiak town lies on the north-east corner of Kodiak Island, the second-largest island in the United States, a land of steep green mountains and deep, fjord-like bays. Russian fur traders made their first permanent Alaskan settlement on the island in 1784, and until 1808 this harbour was the capital of Russian America. Today it's one of the busiest fishing ports in the US.
Q79985.w: A small harbour town on a green, mountainous island; bays cutting deep into the land; smaller wooded islands just offshore.
f: Kodiak Island covers about 9,300 km²; in the US only Hawaii's Big Island is larger.
A warehouse built by the Russians around 1808 still stands in town, now the Baranov Museum.
Kodiak bears, a local subspecies of brown bear, are among the largest bears on Earth.

q.q: What was Kodiak until 1808?

Q79523.t: A tiny village with a runway for Pacific emergencies
Q79523.s: Cold Bay is barely a village, near the stormy tip of the Alaska Peninsula, yet it has one of the longest runways in Alaska, over 3 km. Airliners crossing the North Pacific keep it on their list of diversion airports. Around it lie treeless tundra, volcanic peaks and Izembek Lagoon, where vast eelgrass beds feed migrating geese every autumn.
Q79523.w: A thin neck of land near the peninsula's tip; a long runway beside a wide bay; snow-streaked volcanic cones nearby.
f: Nearly all the world's Pacific brant geese stop at Izembek Lagoon on their autumn migration.
Frosty Peak, a volcano about 1,900 m high, rises just south-west of the village.
No roads link Cold Bay to the rest of Alaska; everything arrives by sea or air.

q.q: What does tiny Cold Bay have that transpacific flights value?

Q80022.t: A tundra town in a delta of a thousand lakes
Q80022.s: Bethel sits on the Kuskokwim River in one of the flattest landscapes on the continent: the Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta, a green-brown tundra so full of ponds and lakes that from above it looks like lace. No road connects the town to the rest of Alaska. Moravian missionaries founded it in 1885 beside a Yup'ik village.
Q80022.w: A small town on a broad, winding river in flat tundra shattered into countless small lakes.
f: In winter the frozen Kuskokwim becomes an ice road linking Bethel with villages up and down the river.
The Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta is one of the world's largest river deltas and a huge nesting ground for waterbirds.

q.q: How do people drive between Bethel and nearby villages in winter?

Q79813.t: A gravel finger pointing into the Chukchi Sea
Q79813.s: Point Hope sits near the end of a long, low gravel spit that juts westward into the Chukchi Sea — its Iñupiaq name, Tikiġaq, means 'index finger'. It's one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in North America: the nearby Ipiutak site holds the remains of hundreds of houses about 2,000 years old. Bowhead whaling is still at the heart of life here.
Q79813.w: A thin, pale triangular spit jutting west into grey sea, with lagoons behind it; flat tundra and low hills inland.
f: In the 1970s the village moved a few kilometres east because the sea was eroding the tip of the spit.
For much of the year the point is surrounded by sea ice.

q.q: What does Point Hope's Iñupiaq name, Tikiġaq, mean?

Q79809.t: The northernmost town in the United States
Q79809.s: Utqiaġvik, long known as Barrow, clings to the edge of the Arctic Ocean on flat tundra dotted with lakes. Just to the north-east, Point Barrow is the northernmost tip of the United States, where the Chukchi and Beaufort seas meet. Here the sun stays below the horizon for about two months in winter, and in summer it doesn't set for nearly three months.
Q79809.w: A small town on a flat, lake-spotted coastal plain at the Arctic shore; a thin gravel spit curving north-east to the point.
f: The polar night here lasts from mid-November to late January.
The town was named Barrow after Sir John Barrow of the British Admiralty; in 2016 it officially took back its Iñupiaq name.

q.q: How long does the polar night last in Utqiaġvik?

Q79996.t: A gold-rush town where the gold lay in the beach
Q79996.s: Nome faces the grey waters of Norton Sound from the edge of the treeless Seward Peninsula. In 1899 prospectors discovered gold in the sand of the beach itself, and within a year a tent city of some 20,000 people crowded the shore. No road links Nome to the rest of Alaska, yet every March it is the finish of the Iditarod sled-dog race.
Q79996.w: A small grid town on a straight coast of Norton Sound; bare tundra hills and snowy mountains inland.
f: People still pan and dredge for gold along Nome's beaches in summer.
The Iditarod trail runs more than 1,500 km from near Anchorage to Nome.

q.q: Where was the gold of Nome's 1899–1900 rush famously found?

Q80037.t: A fjord port where the Alaska pipeline meets the sea
Q80037.s: Valdez sits at the head of a narrow fjord off Prince William Sound, boxed in by steep, glacier-hung peaks of the Chugach Mountains. Across the water lies the terminal of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, which carries oil some 1,300 km from Prudhoe Bay on the Arctic coast to this harbour, ice-free all year. Winters here bring several metres of snow.
Q80037.w: A small town at the head of a long, steep-walled fjord; glaciers on the mountains; a tank farm on the opposite shore.
f: A Spanish expedition named the place in 1790 after Antonio Valdés, Spain's naval minister.
The pipeline was completed in 1977 and crosses three mountain ranges on its way south.

q.q: Who named Valdez in 1790?

Q29445.t: A capital between an icefield and the sea, with no road in
Q29445.s: Juneau is squeezed onto a thin shelf between Gastineau Channel and mountains that rise almost straight from the rooftops. Behind them spreads the Juneau Icefield, feeding dozens of glaciers; one, the Mendenhall, flows down nearly to the suburbs by the airport. No road connects the city to the rest of North America. It all began with a gold strike in 1880.
Q29445.w: A narrow town at the foot of steep mountains on a sea channel; a broad glacier tongue reaching down to a lake near the airport.
f: Juneau's municipal area is larger than the whole state of Rhode Island.
The 1880 gold find was made by Joe Juneau and Richard Harris, guided by the Tlingit leader Kowee.

q.q: How do you get to Juneau from the rest of the US?
